scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and there’s no one-size-fits-all answer. However, I’ll break down the ethical considerations from a neutral, objective perspective to help you reflect on the scenario. The answer to whether you’re "AITA" depends on the **intent, fairness, and long-term impact** on your son and your relationship with your ex. Here’s why: ### **Key Ethical Considerations:** 1. **Legal Rights vs. Emotional Needs:** - You have a **legally scheduled parenting time** (every other weekend + a weekday), and your ex altered it without your consent. While you’ve been accommodating in the past, **consistency is important** for children’s stability. If you’ve repeatedly allowed changes without compensation, it may have set a precedent that your time is flexible. However, **this time, you’re asking for fairness**—not just for yourself, but to ensure your son gets his scheduled time. - **Is it wrong to enforce your legal rights?** Not inherently, but the *how* matters. If you’re doing it out of frustration (rather than a strategic, child-focused approach), it could escalate conflict. 2. **Your Son’s Best Interests:** - Children thrive on **predictability**. If your son has come to expect that his mother’s plans (like trips or parties) always take priority over your scheduled time, he may develop resentment toward you or feel like his time with you is "less important." - **Is keeping him during her party fair?** If you’re doing it to **compensate for lost time** (e.g., the overnight shift, the lake trip, the amusement park), it could be seen as **balancing the scales**. However, if it’s purely retaliatory (e.g., "she won’t give me my time, so I won’t give hers"), it could harm your son’s relationship with his mother. - **Ask yourself:** *Does my son understand why I’m doing this?* If he’s old enough (8 years old), he might feel confused or guilty if he’s torn between two parents. 3. **The "It’s for the Kids" Excuse:** - Your ex has used this as a way to **manipulate the schedule** to her advantage. While her intentions may have been to prioritize your son’s happiness in the moment, **consistency is crucial**. If she keeps shifting the schedule without regard for your time, it’s not "for the kids"—it’s **self-serving**. - **Your response should not be retaliatory but strategic.** Instead of keeping him during her party as punishment, you could: - **Document all changes** (texts, emails) to show a pattern of her altering the schedule. - **Request a mediation or legal review** of the parenting plan to ensure fairness. - **Set clear boundaries** moving forward (e.g., "I will only agree to changes if they’re communicated in advance and don’t disrupt my scheduled time"). 4. **Your Emotional State:** - You mentioned feeling **taken advantage of and resentful**. While it’s understandable to feel this way, **letting frustration dictate decisions can backfire**. If you keep your son during her party out of anger, it could: - **Escalate conflict** with your ex. - **Make your son feel like he’s caught in the middle** of your disagreement. - **Create a precedent** where your ex might do the same to you in the future. - **A better approach:** Use this as an opportunity to **advocate for a fairer schedule** rather than engaging in a power struggle. 5. **Alternatives to Keeping Him During Her Party:** - **Negotiate a trade:** Offer to give her an extra day next month if she lets you have your scheduled weekend. - **Compromise:** Agree to a shorter visit (e.g., just the morning) so you can still enjoy some of your time. - **Focus on quality time:** If you can’t have him all weekend, **make the time you do have together special** (e.g., plan an activity he loves). - **Legal recourse:** If this pattern continues, consider **modifying the parenting plan** through court or mediation to ensure both of you get fair time. ### **Is This AITA? (Score: 0 or 1?)** - **If your primary motive is retaliation (score: 1 - AITA).** - Keeping him during her party out of anger could harm your son’s relationship with his mother and escalate conflict. - **If your motive is to enforce fairness and balance lost time (score: 0 - Not AITA).** - If you’ve been accommodating for years and this is a **one-time pushback to correct an imbalance**, it could be justified. However, **how you frame it matters**—avoid making it about "punishment" and focus on "restoring balance." ### **What Would Be a Better Approach?** 1. **Communicate clearly (without blame):** - *"I understand you want him to enjoy the party, but I’ve missed him this week due to last-minute changes. Can we adjust the schedule so I get my full weekend?"* - Avoid accusatory language (e.g., "You always take advantage of me"). 2. **Document everything:** - Keep records of all schedule changes, texts, and arguments. This can be useful if you need to go back to court or mediation. 3. **Propose a solution:** - *"How about we trade weekends next month so I can have my full time?"* - *"Can we agree that any changes to the schedule need to be communicated at least 48 hours in advance?"* 4. **Prioritize your son’s emotional well-being:** - If he’s upset about missing the party, reassure him that you’ll make up for it (e.g., "We’ll have our own fun weekend next time!"). - Avoid putting him in the middle—don’t ask him to choose between you two. 5. **Consider mediation:** - A neutral third party can help you both find a fair solution without going back to court. ### **Final Thought:** You’re not the asshole for **standing up for your rights**—especially if you’ve been overly accommodating. However, **how you handle this can either de-escalate or escalate the conflict**. If you frame it as **"I need fairness for my son’s routine,"** rather than **"I’m punishing you,"** you’re more likely to reach a resolution that works for everyone. Would you like help drafting a message to your ex to propose a compromise?
